newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: FOCUS - PHILIPS IN RED IN 1996 BUT SEES RECOVERY.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - PHILIPS IN RED IN 1996 BUT SEES RECOVERY.

text.p: Philips Electronics NV on Thursday reported its first net annual loss since 1992, hit by huge restructuring and one-off charges and buffeted by stubbornly difficult market conditions, but vowed profits would return to customary levels in 1997.

The Dutch electronics giant, whose product range spans shavers to semiconductors, reported a 1996 net loss of 590 million guilders compared to a 1995 net profit of 2.52 billion guilders, after net extraordinary charges of 1.3 billion.
Net profit from normal operations amounted to 723 million guilders, down from 2.68 billion in 1995, and way below the range of analysts' forecasts of 1.09 billion to 1.53 billion guilders profit.

The dividend was held unchanged at 1.60 guilders per common share. "We have decided to pay a dividend equal to last year's because we are confident that we will produce a result in 1997 which is in line with normal expectations," said Cor Boonstra, addressing his first annual results news conference since becoming chairman in October last year.
"The year 1996 was a severe disappointment, due to a much lower level of sales growth and costs which grew at a faster rate than sales," Philips said in a statement.
However, the company anticipated its current businesses would continue to grow in 1997.
"We are committed to a return to profitability and to the achievement of a positive cash flow of over one billion guilders," Boonstra said.
He acknowledged the effect of the extraordinaries and added Philips had not responded quickly enough to market conditions.
"Part of this decline was caused by gearing up our organisation for growth which did not materialise. We were simply not quick enough in reacting to the market," he said.
"We do not blame the markets, nor our competitors, but rather take full responsibility for our lack of speed," he said.

Charges taken during the year included an 800 million guilder pre-tax charge to restructure the Sound and Vision unit as well as one billion guilders -- of which 600 million related to loss making German unit Grundig .
Philips has deconsolidated its Grundig unit and will from this year no longer pick up the tab for losses at the company, accounting for it on a pro-rata basis for its 32 percent stake.
Philips is currently focusing on existing core businesses rather than moving into new areas.
"At this stage we are focusing on building our 100 existing businesses, rather than acquiring businesses in new areas or strategically reshaping the portfolio," Boonstra said.
Boonstra reiterated his policy of weeding out the company's underperformers and loss-makers.
"While this process is not yet complete, it is on schedule, and we are rapidly disposing of actvities that absorb profits, cash and management time," he said.

He poured cold water on speculation swirling around financial markets that he was preparing to split the company up. Market watchers and some analysts have speculated that Boonstra might be tempted to fulfil his target of maximising value to Philips shareholders by splitting up the company and going forward in a drastically pared down format.
Boonstra said the relationship with 75 percent-owned music and films group PolyGram NV was not under review, tackling speculation the unit would be put up for sale.
He reiterated Philips' commitment to its troubled Sound and Vision unit, which makes televisions and audio equipment.
"There's not a serious consideration, there's not even an unserious consideration, to change our relationship with Sound and Vision," he told the results news conference.
Philips made a fourth quarter net loss from normal operations of 81 million guilders versus a profit of 1.02 billion guilders in the fourth quarter of 1995.
Analysts had expected Philips to report fourth quarter net profit from normal operations of 387-750 million guilders, with consensus around 526 million.

"The figures were not as good as expected, but not terribly disappointing. It is a good idea Philips is taking all the charges now... 1997 will probably still be tough, but in 1998 the effects of all the restructuring should start working out for Philips," said Peter Wortel of Delta Lloyd Bank.

Eric de Graaf of ING Barings said his firm was sticking to its buy recommendation. "We believe in the sector and we think that Boonstra is walking the right path. If he cuts away the bad parts, the rest will be good," he said.
Shares in Philips initially hovered around Wednesday's closing level of 78.10 guilders after the results came out but by 1200 GMT the shares were off 30 cents to 77.80 guilders.
